summary: In C programming, printf is used to display output on the screen and scanf is used to read input from the user, both relying on format specifiers to handle different data types.
shortNotes: printf() prints formatted output to the console; it is defined in the stdio.h header file.
scanf() reads formatted input from the keyboard; it also requires stdio.h.
Format specifiers like %d (int), %f (float), and %c (char) tell the functions what type of data to handle.
scanf() requires the address of the variable using the & (ampersand) operator, e.g., scanf("%d", &num);
\n is a newline escape sequence used inside printf to move the cursor to the next line.
Always include #include <stdio.h> at the top of your program when using printf or scanf.

detailed.explanation:
In C, the two most basic tools for interacting with users are `printf` and `scanf`. Both are functions provided by the standard input/output library, which you include at the top of your program using `#include <stdio.h>`. Without this line, the compiler will not recognise these functions.

`printf` stands for *print formatted*. It is used to display text and variable values on the screen. You provide a format string in double quotes, which can contain plain text and format specifiers. For example, `printf("Age: %d\n", age);` will print the value of the integer variable `age` in place of `%d`. The `\n` at the end moves the cursor to the next line.

`scanf` stands for *scan formatted*. It reads input typed by the user and stores it in a variable. The key rule is that you must pass the *address* of the variable using the `&` operator. For example, `scanf("%d", &age);` reads an integer and stores it at the memory location of `age`. Forgetting `&` is one of the most common beginner mistakes.

Format specifiers are codes that begin with `%` and indicate the data type. The most common ones are: `%d` for `int`, `%f` for `float`, `%lf` for `double`, `%c` for `char`, and `%s` for strings. Using the wrong specifier can cause unexpected output or even a crash.

Escape sequences like `\n` (newline), `\t` (tab), and `\\` (backslash) are special character combinations used inside string literals to control formatting. They are written with a backslash prefix and are interpreted by the compiler, not printed literally.

definitions.meaning: A standard library function in C used to print formatted text and variable values to the console.
A standard library function in C used to read formatted input from the keyboard and store it in variables.
A placeholder starting with % used inside printf and scanf to indicate the data type, e.g., %d for integer.
A combination of a backslash and a character used inside strings to represent special characters, like \n for newline.
An operator used in scanf to pass the memory address of a variable so the function knows where to store the input.
The standard input/output header file in C that must be included to use printf and scanf.

points: Always write #include <stdio.h> at the top of any C program that uses printf or scanf.
Use %d for int, %f for float, %lf for double, %c for char, and %s for strings.
In scanf, always use the & operator before a variable name (except for strings/arrays).
\n inside a printf string moves output to the next line; it does not print a visible character.
printf returns the number of characters printed; scanf returns the number of items successfully read — these are rarely used by beginners but good to know for exams.
Mismatched format specifiers and variable types lead to undefined behaviour — always match them correctly.
Multiple values can be read in one scanf call: scanf("%d %d", &a, &b); reads two integers.
For printing a float with 2 decimal places, use %.2f inside printf, e.g., printf("%.2f", price);.

codeExample.explanation:
Line 1: #include <stdio.h> includes the standard I/O library so printf and scanf are available.
Line 3: main() is the entry point of every C program.
Lines 4-6: Three variables are declared — age (int), marks (float), and grade (char).
Line 9: printf prints a prompt asking the user to enter their age.
Line 10: scanf reads an integer from the keyboard and stores it in age using &age.
Line 12-13: Same pattern for marks using %f for float.
Line 15-16: A space before %c in scanf skips any leftover whitespace (like a newline) from previous input.
Lines 19-22: printf displays each variable using matching format specifiers. %.2f prints marks rounded to 2 decimal places.
Line 24: return 0 signals successful program termination.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the & operator in scanf, e.g., writing scanf("%d", num) instead of scanf("%d", &num). This causes undefined behaviour because scanf does not know where to store the value.
Using the wrong format specifier, such as using %d to read or print a float variable. Always match %f with float and %d with int.
Forgetting #include <stdio.h> at the top of the program, which causes a compilation error because the compiler cannot find the definitions of printf and scanf.

questions.prompt: Which header file must be included to use printf and scanf in C?
questions.explanation: printf and scanf are declared in the standard input/output header file stdio.h. Without it, the compiler will give an error.

questions.prompt: What is the correct format specifier for reading a float value using scanf?
questions.explanation: For float variables, %f is the correct format specifier in both printf and scanf. %lf is used for double.

questions.prompt: What does the escape sequence \n do inside a printf string?
options: Moves the cursor to the next line
questions.explanation: \n is a newline escape sequence. When printf encounters it, the cursor moves to the beginning of the next line on the console.

questions.prompt: Which of the following scanf statements is CORRECT for reading an integer into variable x?
questions.explanation: scanf requires the address of the variable using the & operator. The format string comes first, followed by &x.

questions.prompt: What will printf("%.2f", 3.14159); display on the screen?
questions.explanation: %.2f rounds and displays the float value to exactly 2 decimal places, so 3.14159 is displayed as 3.14.

questions.prompt: Which format specifier is used to print a single character using printf?
questions.explanation: %c is the format specifier for a single character (char data type) in both printf and scanf.

questions.prompt: Why is the & operator required in scanf but not in printf?
questions.answer: scanf needs to store the value entered by the user into a variable, so it requires the memory address of that variable using &. printf only reads the value of the variable to display it, so the address is not needed.
questions.explanation: printf just reads the value to print it. scanf must write a new value into the variable, so it needs to know the exact memory location, which & provides.

questions.prompt: What are format specifiers in C? Give two examples.
questions.answer: Format specifiers are special codes starting with % used in printf and scanf to indicate the data type of the value being printed or read. For example, %d is used for integers and %f is used for float values.
questions.explanation: Format specifiers act as placeholders. They tell the function which type of data to expect, ensuring the correct binary interpretation of the value.
printf evaluates x + y which is 5 + 3 = 8, and prints it as an integer using %d. No newline is added, so the output is simply 8.

questions.prompt: Write a C program that asks the user to enter two integers, reads them using scanf, and then prints their sum using printf.
questions.explanation: We declare two integer variables a and b. We use printf to prompt the user, then scanf with %d %d and &a, &b to read both integers. Finally, printf prints the sum using %d with the expression a + b.

scenes.title: Welcome: What is Input and Output in C?

steps.say: Hello everyone, welcome to this lesson on input and output in C programming. Today we will learn how to talk to the user, how to show information on the screen, and how to read what the user types.
In C, we use two special functions for this. printf is used to print output, and scanf is used to read input from the keyboard.
Both these functions come from a library called stdio dot h, which we must include at the top of every program.
Think of printf as the program speaking to the user, and scanf as the program listening.
Let us look at printf first. To print a simple message, we write printf followed by the message in double quotes.
Here is our main function. Inside it, we write our printf statement.
This line prints the message Hello World on the screen. The backslash n at the end moves the cursor to a new line.
To print a variable value, we use a format specifier. Percent d is for integers. The variable name comes after a comma.
So percent d is replaced by the value of age when the program runs. This gives us Age colon 20 on the screen.
Now let us learn scanf. This function reads what the user types and stores it in a variable.
Here we declare an integer variable called num. Then we print a prompt asking the user to enter a number.
Now comes scanf. Notice we write ampersand num, not just num. The ampersand gives scanf the memory address of the variable so it knows where to save the value.
Finally we print back what the user entered to confirm it.
Forgetting the ampersand in scanf is the most common mistake. Always remember ampersand before the variable name in scanf.
Let us quickly go over the important format specifiers you need to know. These are used in both printf and scanf.
Percent d is for int, percent f is for float, and percent l f is for double.
Percent c is for a single character, and percent s is for a string of characters.
If you want to print a float with only two decimal places, use dot two f inside your printf format string.
This will print 3 point 1 4. The dot two controls how many decimal places are shown.
Great work today. Let us quickly recap what we have learned in this lesson.
First, always include stdio dot h at the top of your program to use printf and scanf.
Use printf to show output on the screen, and use the correct format specifier for the data type.
Use scanf to read input from the user, and always put ampersand before the variable name.
Match your format specifiers carefully. Percent d for int, percent f for float, and percent c for char. See you in the next lesson!
